header:
GDP: what it counts
and what it misses

lines.text: Mowing your own lawn? GDP values it at $0.
lines.say: Mowing your own lawn? GDP values it at zero.

lines.text: GDP adds up the market value of the final goods and services a country produces.
lines.say: GDP adds up the market value of the final goods and services a country produces.

lines.text: In 2025, US GDP was about $30.9 trillion.
lines.say: In twenty twenty-five, US GDP was about thirty point nine trillion dollars.
After inflation, it grew two point three percent in twenty twenty-five.

lines.text: The only drop here was 2020, the pandemic year: -2.1%.
lines.say: The only drop here was twenty twenty, the pandemic year: minus two point one percent.

lines.text: Before the inflation adjustment, our math says it grew about 5%, so over half was higher prices.
lines.say: Before the inflation adjustment, our math says it grew about five percent, so over half was higher prices.

lines.text: GDP counts paid work, like a hired lawn crew or crash repairs, but it misses unpaid chores, free time and pollution.
lines.say: GDP counts paid work, like a hired lawn crew or crash repairs, but it misses unpaid chores, free time and pollution.

lines.text: A government study found unpaid home work would have added about 26% to 2010 GDP.
lines.say: A government study found unpaid home work would have added about twenty-six percent to twenty ten GDP.

lines.text: National income pioneer Simon Kuznets warned in 1934: it measures size, not well-being.
lines.say: National income pioneer Simon Kuznets warned in nineteen thirty-four: it measures size, not well-being.

post.title: GDP: what it counts and the work it misses
post.ig:
Mow your own lawn and GDP values that work at $0. Hire a crew and it counts.
US GDP was $30.86 trillion in 2025, about $30.9 trillion (BEA, as revised Sept 2026).
Real growth was 2.3% in 2025; before the inflation adjustment, about 5% (our math), so over half of nominal growth was higher prices.
A 2012 BEA study found unpaid household work would have added about 26% to GDP in 2010.
GDP measures the size of an economy, not well-being.
Sources: BEA (via FRED), BEA Survey of Current Business (2012).
